architectural_patterns.justification: The document explicitly describes the system as using a microservices architecture, where services are deployed in Docker containers and managed by Traefik. This aligns with the definition of microservices, and the explanation provided in the mappings is supported by the document.

The document describes the system as following a client-server model, where the client (browser) requests resources and renders the interface, while the server handles logic and data. This is clearly explained in the mappings, and the document supports this with examples such as the use of Next.js for the client-side rendering and PostgreSQL for the server-side database.

components.justification: The document provides a detailed explanation of the Security Service, including its role as a reverse proxy and load balancer. It mentions that Traefik manages HTTP/HTTPS traffic, enforces secure communication, and routes requests to internal services. The mappings correctly link this component to the relevant requirements, such as secure authentication and compatibility with web browsers.

The document explains that the System Service is built using Next.js, which supports both client-side and server-side rendering. It details how the service interacts with external APIs (e.g., Google OAuth, Stripe, Brevo) and manages user authentication, payments, and email functionalities. The mappings correctly associate this component with the relevant requirements, such as user registration, authentication, and payment processing.

The document describes the Data Service as a PostgreSQL database that stores all application data, including users, companies, products, and routes. It mentions that the database enforces constraints like uniqueness and foreign keys, ensuring data integrity. The mappings correctly link this component to the relevant requirements, such as storing product and company data and enforcing data relationships.

The document explains that the Google OAuth Service is used for user authentication, integrating with external identity providers like Google. It mentions that this service handles secure authentication tokens and callbacks. The mappings correctly associate this component with the relevant requirement of authenticating existing users via email.

The document describes the Amazon S3 Service as a cloud storage solution for storing images of products and users. It mentions that this service provides scalable and secure storage for uploaded files. The mappings correctly link this component to the relevant requirement of saving all images of products/users.

The document explains that the Stripe Service is used for processing payments, including subscription plans and product return fees. It mentions that this service handles webhooks for subscription changes and processes payments securely. The mappings correctly associate this component with the relevant requirements, such as handling payments for product returns and subscription plans.

The document describes the Brevo Service as a tool for sending transactional emails, such as MagicLinks for user authentication. It mentions that this service manages email communications during the registration process. The mappings correctly link this component to the relevant requirement of registering new users and authenticating existing users via email.

The document explains that the Sentry Service is used for monitoring and tracking errors and exceptions in the application. It mentions that this service helps maintain uptime and recover from failures quickly. The mappings correctly associate this component with the relevant requirement of achieving 99.9% uptime and recovering from failures in less than 1 hour.

The document describes Docker as a containerization platform that packages and runs application services, facilitating horizontal scaling and simplifying deployment and maintenance. The mappings correctly link this component to the relevant requirements of scalability and ease of maintenance.

design_patterns.justification: The document explains that the UI is built using reusable components, promoting modularity and maintainability. It mentions that these components encapsulate their own logic, styles, and state. The mappings correctly associate this design pattern with the relevant requirement of having an intuitive and easy-to-use interface.

The document describes the use of event listeners (observer pattern) to update the UI in response to state changes. It mentions that observers subscribe to a subject to receive notifications of state changes, ensuring responsive UI updates. The mappings correctly link this design pattern to the relevant requirement of having an intuitive and easy-to-use interface.

The document explains that the Prisma Client is implemented as a singleton to ensure only one instance exists, preventing multiple database connections. This is crucial for maintaining stability during development and hot-reload. The mappings correctly associate this design pattern with the relevant requirement of achieving 99.9% uptime and recovering from failures quickly.
